chunks: CMOS and the CMOS buffer. The question: What is CMOS? Draw a CMOS buffer.
CMOS builds logic from pairs of transistors that work as opposites. A PMOS network connects the output to the supply, and an NMOS network connects it to ground.
For any steady input, exactly one network is on. A CMOS buffer is two inverters in a row, which cleans up a signal and adds drive strength.
Imagine a see-saw with a person at each end. When one end is down touching the ground, the other end is up. They are never both down.
A CMOS stage is like that: either the output is tied up to the supply or tied down to ground, and never both at once (apart from a brief moment while it switches).
This is why no steady current flows from supply to ground.
PMOS source on V DD, NMOS source on ground, gates shorted together as the input, drains shorted together as the output.
For either steady input, one transistor is off, so there is no DC path between the rails.
CMOS: complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, using both PMOS and NMOS together. Inverter: a gate whose output is the opposite of its input.
Pull-up / pull-down: connecting the output to the supply, or to ground. Rail: a supply line, V DD or ground.
Buffer: a stage that outputs the same logic value, with more drive strength.
Use a 3. 3 volts supply. In the inverter, an input of 3. 3 volts turns the NMOS on and the PMOS off, so the output goes to 0 volts.
An input of 0 volts turns the PMOS on and the NMOS off, so the output goes to 3. 3 volts. Now chain two inverters.
The first flips the signal and the second flips it back, so the output equals the input. The second one is often bigger, so it can drive a heavier load. That is the whole idea.

"CMOS means complementary MOS: every gate has a PMOS pull-up network to V DD and an NMOS pull-down network to ground, driven by the same inputs, so exactly one side is on at a time and there's no static current.
The basic cell is the inverter: PMOS on top, NMOS on the bottom, gates tied as input, drains tied as output.
A single stage always inverts, so a buffer is two inverters in series, usually with the second one sized up to drive a heavier load."
